<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par88" />appended to the ground-form,<ref>On dual endings appended to the plural see {{GHGpar|87|s}} and {{GHGpar|95|o}} at the beginning.</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם|translate=both hands}}, {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמַ֫יִם|translate=two days}}. In the feminine the dual termination is always added to the old ending ''ath'' (instead of {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}), but necessarily with ''ā'' (since it is in an open syllable before the tone), thus {{GHGheb|text=־ָתַ֫יִם}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׂפָה|translate=lip}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׂפָתַ֫יִם|translate=both lips}}. From a feminine with the ending {{GHGheb|text=־֫ ־ֶת}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נְח֫שֶׁת}} (from ''n<sup>e</sup>ḥušt'') the dual is formed like {{GHGheb|text=נְחֻשְׁתַּ֫יִם|translate=double fetters}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|b}}
With nouns which in the singular have not a feminine ending, the dual termination is likewise really added to the ground-form; but the latter generally undergoes certain changes in consequence of the shifting of the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּנָף|translate=wing}} (ground-form ''kănăph''), dual {{GHGheb|text=כְּנָפַ֫יִם}}, the first ''ă'' becoming {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, since it no longer stands before the tone, and the second ''ă'' being lengthened before the new tone-syllable. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=16|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=23}}b the form {{GHGheb|text=כִּכְּרַ֫יִם}} (which should be {{GHGheb|text=כִּכָּרַ֫יִם}}) evidently merely points to the ''constr. st''. {{GHGheb|text=כִּכְּרֵי}}, which would be expected before {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫סֶף}}; cf. {{GHGheb|text=כִּכָּרָ֑יִם}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=23}} a, and on the syntax see {{GHGpar|131|d}}. In the segholate forms ({{GHGpar|84|a|a}}) the dual ending is mostly added to the ground-form, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫גֶל|translate=foot}} (ground-form ''răgl''), dual {{GHGheb|text=רַגְלַ֫יִם}}; cf., however, {{GHGheb|text=קְרָנַ֫יִם}} (only in the book of Daniel), as well as {{GHGheb|text=קַרְנַ֫יִם}} from {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫רֶן|translate=horn}}, and {{GHGheb|text=לְחָיַ֫יִם}} from {{GHGheb|text=לְחִי|translate=cheek}} (as if from the plurals {{GHGheb|text=קְרָנוֹת}}, {{GHGheb|text=לִחָיִם}}).—A feminine dual of an adjective used substantivally occurs in {{GHGheb|text=עֲצַלְתַּ֫יִם|translate=a sluggish pair}} (of hands) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=18}} from the sing. {{GHGheb|text=עָצֵל}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|c}}
Rem. 1. Certain place-names were formerly reckoned as dual-forms (so in earlier editions of this Grammar, and still in König’s {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgebäude}}, ii. 437), viz.— (''a'') those in {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתַ֫יִן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=17a}} (locative {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתָ֑יְּנָה}}, but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=17b|hidebook=completely}} {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתָ֑ן}}), and {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתָן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=קַרְתָּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=21|verse=32}}, identical with {{GHGheb|text=קִרְיָתַ֫יִם}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=6|verse=61}} (cf. also the Moabite names of towns in the Mêša‛ inscription, line 10 {{GHGheb|text=קריתן}} = Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=קִרְיָתַ֫יִם}}; line 30 {{GHGheb|text=בת דבלתן}} = {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית דִּבְלָתַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=22}}; lines 31, 32 {{GHGheb|text=חורנן}}={{GHGheb|text=חֹרוֹנַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=15|verse=5}}, &c.); (''b'') in {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=34}} {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעֵינָם}} ( = {{GHGheb|text=עֵינַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=21}}). The view that {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}} arise from a contraction of the dual terminations {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִן}} (as in Western Aramaic, cf. also nom. ''âni'', accus. ''aini'', of the dual in Arabic) and {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִם}} seemed to be supported by the Mêša‛; inscription, where we find (line 20) {{GHGheb|text=מאתן|translate=two hundred}} = {{GHGheb|text=מָאתַ֫יִן}}, Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=מָאתַ֫יִם}}. But in many of these supposed duals either a dual sense cannot be detected at all, or it does not agree at any rate with the nature of the Semitic dual, as found elsewhere. Hence it can hardly be doubted that {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִם}} in these place-names only arise from a subsequent expansion of the terminations {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}: so Wellhausen, ''Jahrbücher für Deutsche Theologie'', xxi. 433; Philippi, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xxxii. 65 f.; Barth, {{GHGcite|title=Nominalbildung}}, p. 319, note 5; Strack, ''Kommentar zur Genesis'', p. 135. The strongest argument in favour of this opinion is that we have a clear case of such an expansion in the ''Q<sup>e</sup>rê perpetuum'' ({{GHGpar|17|c}}) {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשָׁלַ֫יִם}} for {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשָׂלֵם}} (so, according to Strack, even in old MSS. of the ''Mišna''; cf. ''Urusalim'' in the Tel-el-Amarna tablets, and the Aramaic form {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשְׁלֵם}}): similarly in<section end="par88" /><noinclude>
